When someone says, ‘You’re creative people, but I’m more down-to-earth,’ I’m convinced that they’re suppressing something in themselves. For whatever reason – shame, fear, or social conditioning – they don’t allow themselves to recognize the artist within.

I truly believe we’re all creators to some degree. And if someone reading this thinks, ‘No, that definitely isn’t me,’ I’d suggest simply opening yourself up to the world a little more. There is definitely something inside you.
How would you suggest people reconnect with that creative part of themselves?

Xenia: There’s a practice called "Impulse". For instance, you’re walking down the street and suddenly feel like picking up a leaf or photographing a particular building. Your inner critic immediately says, ‘Why? Nobody needs this. We’re late. Please stop doing something pointless.

But that little impulse is exactly what your mind is telling you to ignore. If you listen to this impulse once, then again and again, the world gradually becomes richer – and you learn more about yourself, what you genuinely like, and what you really want to do.

The important thing is to hear that voice saying, ‘This is pointless,’ and answer: ‘Great. I’m going to do something pointless.’ That helped me enormously. It’s actually what led me to art school, because at first, studying art felt completely pointless.
Elena, do you have your own way of unlocking that creative part of yourself?

Elena: I’m a very slow person, so observation helps me a lot. I love immersing myself in the process – looking at a tree, feeling the wind. Simply observing yourself and the world around you can reveal a lot.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt4lmobma8gvmc.mp4
content.caption: Fragment of the Installation for Tales Wedding Planner

content.content: What is your favorite place in Lisbon, somewhere you always want to return to?

Elena: Probably the Gulbenkian Garden. It’s an incredible park and museum. It’s right in the city, but once you enter, it feels like you’re somewhere completely different. It’s a beautiful combination of nature, architecture, and art. You walk in and suddenly find yourself in your own little world. You can breathe out.

Xenia: For me, besides Gulbenkian, it’s probably Cabo Espichel. It has this incredible lighthouse and is considered by the Portuguese to be one of the westernmost points of Europe. I also love the café at Museu Albuquerque, and MACAM – Museu de Arte Contemporânea Armando Martins – has a wonderful café too. They’re all affordable but incredibly stylish. Museums often have amazing cafés.

alts: Gulbenkian Garden
Gulbenkian Garden
Cabo Espichel
Cafe in Foundation Albuquerque

content.content: What has been your most inspiring trip?
Xenia: I’ve just come back from New York, where my husband and I got married, so that’s definitely my strongest impression at the moment. But I think every journey is inspiring in its own way.

Elena: Recently, it was my solo trip to Porto. I visited the Serralves Museum of Contemporary Art, explored Álvaro Siza’s architecture, and absolutely loved it. The fact that I went alone also made it a special experience.
Finally, what is the one piece of advice you would give every reader?
Elena: Keep doing what you genuinely love. Despite your inner limitations, look deeply within yourself, listen to your true desires, and simply give yourself permission to pursue them.

Xenia: The main lesson I took from art school is: ‘Experience resistance.’ If you feel resistance toward something, you should move toward it. It means there’s a huge amount of energy hidden there. Don’t ignore or suppress it – look at it more closely.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt35850in1olvy.mp4
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt35cexjfquvyg.mp4
content.caption: Installation for Tales Wediding Planner

articles.title: Where We Meet Ourselves - interview with Keisuke Azuma
articles.author: Maria Ivanova
articles.excerpt: Artist Keisuke Azuma on washing paint back off the canvas, the Japanese aesthetics of shadow and emptiness behind his work, and why art has no right to be exclusive.

content.content: Born in Japan, trained in London, and now based in Lithuania, Keisuke Azuma builds his canvases by taking away rather than adding – washing pigment back, dissolving the body until only a hand, a foot, or a fragment of gesture survives against raw, unfinished canvas. His recent series, currently on show in KIAF Seoul,  and exhibited recently in solo shows in New York and Paris, strips the human figure down to its most universal parts, leaving the rest as an invitation: a blank the viewer fills with their own reflection.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8oisq6xlwmv4.jpg
content.caption: Keisuke Azuma in his studio

content.content: Epris met Azuma over a video call from his studio in Vilnius, where he lives with his wife and their dog and cat. Below you can find our conversation on the Japanese aesthetics of deduction that shaped his method and why he thinks art has no right to be exclusive.
01 · Becoming a painter
Maria Ivanova [MA]: What was the starting point for you to become an artist – were you immersed in art from childhood, or did the desire come later?

Keisuke Azuma [KA]: It's always a funny story, because I never actually wanted to be an artist. I loved art, obviously – I read a lot about artists from the Baroque period, and it always said they were poor. There were exceptions, but in general it looked like such a difficult profession. Still, I loved it, even though I was pretty much alone in that in my community. No one else in my family cared about art.

I was doing marketing work in a shop, and someone asked if I could do an illustration. I saw how customers reacted, and I was fascinated by that power art has to deliver a concept. I was into film too, so for a while I thought I'd combine the two through illustration. That's why I chose art school in the first place. During my studies I found this other love – expressing my own words, my own sense of identity. So it was a gradual thing. I kept trying to make excuses not to be a painter, and I kept coming back to it anyway.

Eventually I started showing in London while I was still studying, and having a gallery or two consign my work convinced me it might actually be possible. My wife's support mattered enormously too – she married me knowing I wanted to be an artist. That's how I built myself into one.
I kept trying to make excuses not to be a painter, and I kept coming back to it anyway.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8omin9z9m7tf.jpg
content.caption: Soliloquy, Keisuke Azuma, 2026, oil on canvas

content.content: MI: Do you think that pull toward art is something innate, or something your surroundings gave you?

KA: It feels a bit cheeky to just say “I was born this way,” but – my mother is an architect. My sister collages, just for her own journaling. My father doesn't do anything art-related, and neither does anyone else in the family, really. So I'd say it's more innate than not, with maybe a small hint of it in the bloodline. I actually tried hard not to go this way. In high school an art teacher personally called me to join his club, and I told him I wanted to do music instead. There was always a little sign pointing at it, even when I wasn't looking for one.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8ooivc2dg67b.jpg
content.caption: Ring, Keisuke Azuma, 2025, oil on canvas

content.content: 02 · Method
MI: You were born and raised in Japan, then moved to London to study. You've said your work is rooted in Japanese culture – how does that show up in your practice?

KA: There's a book, In Praise of Shadows – about how traditional Japanese houses use light and shadow, with a strong emphasis on negative space. A single shelf holding flowers becomes the whole focal point of a room precisely because everything around it is empty. Even a living space gets treated like a complete art expression. I was already interested in the contrast of light and shadow – I used to take a lot of photographs – and at some point that merged with my painting.

I take classical paintings as a reference, most of the time, and I manipulate them. In the process I try to eliminate elements so I can focus on what actually matters, what I want to deliver. All of my paintings have white space – that's the raw canvas itself. I wash the paint off. It's not perfectly clean; you can still see lines underneath. I do it because I love the physical act of taking the colour back out. In Japanese Zen culture, what matters is minimalist expression, and I wanted an immersive, physical process for myself.
All of my paintings have white space – that's the raw canvas itself. I wash the paint off.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8o4qs3q9q7wi.jpg
content.caption: Most Things in Between, Keisuke Azuma, 2026, Oil on Canvas

content.content: MI: When I first saw your paintings I immediately felt that Japanese influence – that emphasis on essence over material, on how a space makes you feel rather than what's placed in it.

KA: You're right. I once visited a Tadao Ando church – a concrete box with two thin lines of glass standing in for a cross. Walking in, I felt completely safe, precisely because there was nothing there. That kind of minimalist emptiness matters because it's one of the few places left to actually see who we are – we spend so much of our lives on our phones, immersed in content instead. I keep a monotone background in most of my paintings for the same reason: when you wash off paint there are traces everywhere, and every one of them matters. And I still love how Baroque paintings use darkness – not as absence, but as a presence in the frame.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8o6ppz5cm8rs.jpg
content.caption: Church of the Light, Tadao Ando, 1989

content.content: 03 · Metamorphosis
MI: Your recent body of work, Human Metaphors, showed in Paris – it deals with vulnerability, identity, and change. Is it a response to the pressure of constant self-presentation we live under now?

KA: I think so. This series is a statement against that kind of validation-chasing. In London I felt I had to fit a certain format – what's trendy, what's popular, what's seemingly correct. Living in Lithuania changed that. I barely see anyone – my wife, our dog, our cat. Lithuanians, and Slavic people generally in my experience, are very true to themselves. They don't even say hello to me half the time, which I actually find refreshing – there's no pretending. People chase influence and money, and it matters, but at the end of the day you're the most important person in your own life, and it's easy to forget that. That's the question I'm trying to leave in the painting – which is also why I leave so much empty space. It has to become the viewer's own experience.

content.caption: Details of “Soliloquy”, 2026

content.content: MI: Through the abstraction, but with hands and feet still present, are you gesturing at something like consciousness or soul – a self that can be detached from the body?

KA: Exactly. The title Human Metaphors was for the New York show; the Paris one was called Metamorphosis, which I love just as much. I erase the body because I think we've stopped paying attention to it as a physical scale – we live in our heads, on our phones, and the body becomes almost incidental next to the face, which carries the first impression. Hands and feet, though, are strangely universal. Bodies vary enormously, but a hand stays a hand. So I keep them as a kind of anchor – something everyone can recognise – and erase the rest so people can enter the painting without needing permission first.

Contemporary art has become elite-focused in places. Art should be accessible. When I see people say “I hate this painting,” it makes me a little sad, because it's still a human creation, even the ones I personally don't like. So the hands and feet are also an invitation – I don't want anyone standing in front of my work feeling like they don't belong there.
I don't want anyone standing in front of my work feeling like they don't belong there.

content.caption: Union, Keisuke Azuma, 2026, oil on canvas

content.content: 04 · On Eggs Series and A Journey to Abstraction
MI: You have an earlier series titled Eggs, more centre-oriented – something about transformation, maybe rebirth?

KA: Exactly that. After graduating in London I moved straight to Lithuania, into a basement studio, in winter, with nobody around – it felt like an art prison, just me and my art. That's was the moment when I made the Eggs series. Before that I was doing abstract landscape painting, which I loved, but I was following what people said was good without fully expressing myself.

I initially started making art through figurative compositions, working in realism. I wanted to combine this with my abstract expression, Japanese aesthetic, deduction. To do this, Eggs series was very important. In this work I tried to create something out of my landscapes - by folding them or experimenting with their physical form.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8oujwbb5bo1t.jpg
content.caption: Distant Plea, Keisuke Azuma, 2025, oil on canvas

content.content: After Eggs series it tooks roughly eight months to reintroduce realistic elements - hand and feets. Eggs series was a transformation for myself.
MI: Do you think abstraction is the purest form of painting – more powerful because it forces self-reflection rather than reading a figure?

KA: I mostly agree. I remember a Monet retrospective in Kyoto – he's technically figurative, very pictorial, but there was one unfinished canvas from the Water Lilies series on show, barely any colour, just a few strokes. It affected me more than his finished work. That's one of the paintings that broke my resistance to abstraction.

Abstraction also has this democratic quality – it makes people feel like they could do it too, and I think that's valuable, even if it sounds naive. I still believe in the power of high realism, Caravaggio and that kind of work – we still go to the cinema for scale and craft – but abstraction fills a gap between the public and elite realism. It has its own contradictions – some abstract work is just as exclusionary – but at its best, it opens things up.
It has its own contradictions – some abstract work is just as exclusionary – but at its best, it opens things up.

alts: Cradle, Keisuke Azuma, 2025, oil on canvas
Static March, Keisuke Azuma, 2025, oil on canvas

content.content: 05 · Why art should be for everyone
MI: You've said art should have a function. What function, in your view?

KA: Art has always had one, I think. Probably the earliest paintings – the Lascaux cave paintings in France, drawings of cattle – already had a narrative function: “this is what I saw today, this is where the hunting spot is”. We still use illustration that way, in guides and encyclopedias. I love Baroque painting particularly because it moved away from portraits of the powerful and started introducing ordinary civic life. It always have a function to talk about something beyond words. For example, Picasso's Guernica is the extreme version of that – painfully, brutally honest, and it makes me sad every time, it has a function to be against the world.

Art can deliver emotions beyond the skills to understand - books can be more efficient, but maybe some people don't know how to read - and painting can be more universal – it's even older than language itself.
MI: Do you think everyone has an innate capacity to understand art, or is it something learned?

KA: Both, I think, but I lean toward “learned.” I hated abstraction as a kid – I loved realism, and when I first saw work by a well-known abstract painter I genuinely didn't get it. Now I did cried in front of a Rothko.

I do believe everyone has a capacity to understand aesthetic and beauty in general - everyone can learn to recognise beauty in a face or in clothing – it doesn't have to be about painting specifically.

My own family still doesn't really understand my abstraction, but they're supportive. My wife's father, who has no art background, once looked at a painting and said, “Oh, he can draw hands and feet – he must be good.” [laughs] That was very important reaction as well - this connection with a work - even if it only lasts a second.
MI: What was your own first major encounter with a work of art – the moment you thought, this is it?

KA: Probably Rothko, in Tate Britain. I already knew his work, but seeing it in person, in a room that was much darker than the rest of the museum, was different. I felt something beyond humanity – like the painting had taken something out of me. One of the black-and-red canvases, almost like a gate to somewhere else. That's probably the painting that made me want to paint.
06 · In Artist’s Studio
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8wi29ll76qp4.jpg
content.caption: Keisuke Azuma’s studio in Lithuania

content.content: MI: Do you paint daily, or wait for inspiration?

KA: Daily now – I have a lot of shows this year, so I don't have the luxury of waiting anymore. I work on an iPad first, manipulating a classical painting, then come to the studio around lunchtime to paint. I keep notes constantly, mostly title ideas – whenever something occurs to me, I write it down so it's there when I need it.
MI: So the starting point now is memory or emotion, recalled, rather than something you're seeing in the moment?

KA: Largely, yes. I still use classical paintings as inspiration when they can help carry a concept, but recently I've been trying to step slightly away from purely personal memory, toward something more generic – I've started making more explicitly political work lately, thinking about what's happening more broadly rather than only in my own life.
MI: Do you plan meticulously, or let the canvas decide in the moment?

KA: I'd say about half and half. Nothing ever repeats exactly – temperature, texture, everything shifts between the iPad sketch and the actual canvas. The painting I showed you earlier was originally dark blue; I didn't like it, went back to the iPad, mocked up something lighter, and ended up loving the mistake – you can still see the blue underneath. On the iPad everything looks matte and controlled; in reality it gets dirtier, more human. I like that.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8wkn228zqy9o.jpg
content.caption: Keisuke Azuma’s studio

content.content: MI: What's your biggest non-visual source of inspiration?

KA: Honestly, everything, but music and film especially. Even our dog – she has no capacity for overthinking, she's just happy, and there's something inspiring about that raw, unfiltered expression. In film I love things that confuse me – David Lynch, work that leaves a question instead of answering it. In music I listen mostly to instrumental or classical pieces, and to a Japanese band whose lyrics are deliberately mysterious – the mystery does more work than an explanation would.
07 · Favourite Places
MI: Do you have any hidden gems in London that you can share with us. Doesn't need to be art-related. A bar, a bench, a street.

KA: Not exactly hidden, but there's a bar in London, called Nickel Bar, inside a former bank building near Bank station, that they gutted and rebuilt – it looks a bit like Hogwarts inside. Very dark, very spacious, more like a grand hotel lounge than a typical bar, and dark enough that you can actually have a private conversation. I only found out about it near the end of my time in London, and I'd go back for that alone.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8vyjtgoszvir.jpg
content.caption: The Nickel Bar, London

content.content: In Japan, I'd point people toward Nara – everyone goes for the deer and the giant Buddha, but if you climb further up the mountain behind the main temple, maybe twenty minutes past where most tourists stop, there's a much quieter temple with a view over the whole city. It feels like stepping back a few centuries. More generally: any small, minor temple you find on a map rather than a “best of” list – somewhere you're actually allowed to walk inside. Kyoto has thousands of them. If you can get matcha there afterward, even better.
08 · On life
MI: You mentioned earlier how much the move from Japan, through London, to Lithuania shaped you – can you say more about that?

KA: As Japanese, we're raised not to express ourselves too openly. Lithuanians, like a lot of Slavic people in my experience, hold onto their independence fiercely, and value both family and a very solid sense of self at the same time. London never really got under my skin that way – it's too much of a melting pot to leave a single mark. Lithuania taught me how to listen to myself. When I go back to Japan now, once a year, I notice how much self-suppression is baked into daily life there, and it feels strange in a way it didn't used to. I still love the culture deeply, but I needed the distance.
MI: And for someone young who wants to be an artist but is afraid to start?

KA: I believe anyone can be an artist, in principle – sustaining yourself entirely on it is a different, harder question. But it takes real guts and commitment, especially now, when the economics of it are unstable and art isn't something society treats as essential. Nobody hands you the opportunity – you make your own. From my first year at university I was applying to every open call I could find, because I was terrified of graduating with no show history. That network, built early, is what let me keep practicing once I moved abroad.

If art feels optional to you, it might not be the right path – it has to be closer to the centre of things than that. It doesn't matter if you're rich or poor going in. You just have to keep the spirit.

If art feels optional to you, it might not be the right path – it has to be closer to the centre of things than that. It doesn't matter if you're rich or poor going in. You just have to keep the spirit.
MI: If you had to give one piece of life advice, what would it be?

KA: Quit being a people-pleaser. I think a lot of people struggle with that, at different levels. It matters, because we only get one life, and I've heard the same thing from a lot of older people in interviews: just do what you actually want. Knowing your own voice, even in small daily decisions, is the whole thing.
…just do what you actually want. Knowing your own voice, even in small daily decisions, is the whole thing.
This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

articles.title: Museo Nivola: A Museum, a Village and the Memory They Share
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Costantino Nivola left a Sardinian village of masons for New York, worked with Le Corbusier, Sert and Saarinen, and never stopped coming back. The team of his museum, on the hill above Orani, on where a museum ends and a village begins, on the method he left behind, and on what a monographic museum can still become.

content.content: Orani is a village in the Barbagia, the mountainous heart of Sardinia. A road climbs up from the valley, the houses gather along the slope, and just above them, on the hillside, a low white building sits among olive trees and looks back down at the roofs. It is one of the most quietly beautiful small museums in Italy, and it belongs, in the fullest sense of the word, to the place it stands in.

Costantino Nivola was born here in 1911, the son of a mason, and learned the trade on his father’s building sites before the ISIA in Monza and a job as a graphic designer for Olivetti in Milan. In 1939 he left for New York. He met Le Corbusier in 1946, wrapped the wall of the Olivetti showroom on Fifth Avenue in a sand-cast relief in 1954, taught at the Harvard Graduate School of Design at the invitation of Josep Lluís Sert, and spent three years filling Eero Saarinen’s colleges at Yale with carved concrete. And he kept coming home. In 1953 he drew a plan to link every house in Orani with vine pergolas; in 1958 he covered the facade of the village church with a graffito and carried his sculptures out into the streets for three days, with the whole village taking part.

The museum that carries his name has inherited that generosity. It keeps its door open to the village, to contemporary artists, to schoolchildren and to researchers, and it does all of this with rare care and warmth. We are grateful to the team of the Museo Nivola for the time and thought they gave to our four questions: where the museum ends and Orani begins, what is still alive in Nivola’s belief in the union of art and architecture, what a museum in an artist’s birthplace can know, and what they hope the museum will become.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8pvrjpqc76eo.jpg
content.caption: The path along the museum wall, Museo Nivola, Orani. Photo Cedric Dasesson. Courtesy Museo Nivola

content.content: Where, in your view, does the Museo Nivola end and Orani begin? Can the village, its landscape and its inhabitants be considered a continuation of the museum space?

In a place like Orani, given its history and its nature, the border between museum and village is difficult to draw. The museum itself is born in a particular position: on the hill, immersed in the landscape and at the same time facing the slope up which the village climbs. Its architecture does not build a rupture with its context, but continually establishes relations with what surrounds it: the vegetation, the shape of the valley, the spring of Su Càntaru and, above all, the community.

This relation is deeper still if we think of Nivola’s own work, because Orani is a presence that runs through all of his research and is evident in the materials, in his childhood memories, in the experience of his father the mason, in his conception of public space and of the relationship with the social life of a place. In the 1953 project Pergola Village, Nivola imagined connecting the houses of the village, ideally and physically, through vine pergolas, turning the streets into shared social space. In 1958, returning to Orani, he made the graffito on the facade of the church of Nostra Signora d’Itria and brought his sculptures directly into the streets, involving the inhabitants in an experience that goes entirely beyond the traditional model of the exhibition.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8phvon2ihj61.jpg
content.caption: Pergola Village, Vined Orani, plate from Interiors, January 1953. Courtesy Museo Nivola

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8pvrsry2q0bf.jpg
content.caption: The church of Nostra Signora d’Itria, Orani, with the graffito Nivola made on its facade in 1958. Courtesy Museo Nivola

content.content: This is why we like to think that the Museo Nivola does not end at the threshold of the building: the village is not an extension of the museum in the sense of a musealisation of the territory, but rather a living interlocutor.

The challenge is precisely to prevent Orani from becoming a backdrop, or a kind of diffuse museum crystallised in the past. We are interested in continuing to build a relationship in which the museum is part of the life of the village and the village keeps entering the museum, through people, through memory, through educational activities, projects in public space and new forms of cultural production.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8phvyrs11r07.jpg
content.caption: Nivola near the funeral monument to his mother and his brother Giuseppe, Orani, 1958. Photo C. Bavagnoli. Courtesy Museo Nivola

content.content: Nivola called himself a sculptor for architecture, and the phrase was not a modest one. It meant that the sculpture would not arrive after the building, like a piece of furniture.
Nivola believed deeply in the integration of art and architecture. How current is that idea today, and what can it teach new generations of artists, architects and designers?

That is the great topicality of his thought. Today, perhaps, even more than when Nivola began working in this direction. For him, the integration of art and architecture did not simply mean placing a work inside a building or on its facade. It meant conceiving space, matter, function and the experience of whoever would inhabit that space all together. The famous total project.

Nivola worked with some of the great protagonists of modern architecture, trying to overcome the disciplinary separation between artist, architect and designer. His interest was directed at space as an overall experience. Sculpture could become wall, relief could become part of architecture, the courtyard a place of encounter. Even the urban plan was to be an instrument for strengthening social relations.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8phw5rzot1h0.jpg
content.caption: The Olivetti showroom on Fifth Avenue, New York, 1954. Photo H. Namuth. Courtesy Museo Nivola

content.content: Behind the idea of integration between the arts there is something wider still: a conception of art as an instrument capable of affecting the quality of collective life.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8pj4hlw7p230.jpg
content.caption: Relief for the Morse & Stiles colleges, Yale University, 1961, sandcast, concrete, 51 x 45 x 9 cm. Photo P. Pinna. Courtesy Museo Nivola

content.content: Nivola invites us to step out of categories that are too rigid. He invites us to ask for whom a space is designed, who will use it, what relations it will produce. At a moment when architecture, art and design are called to confront environmental and social questions and new ways of inhabiting, his interdisciplinary approach appears surprisingly contemporary.

It is not, of course, a matter of merely reproducing his forms and languages, but of inheriting his method: working through dialogue between disciplines, keeping attention on materials and on context, and considering space as something that can orient behaviours, encounters and forms of community; not as a neutral container.
The collection in Orani is the largest anywhere, but the case for a museum in a village of a few thousand people was never an argument about inventory.
What can a museum located in his place of origin tell us about Costantino Nivola that a major international institution could not tell in the same way?

An international institution can tell Nivola within the dimension of global art history and twentieth-century architecture, reconstruct his relationships with New York, with the Harvard Graduate School of Design, with architects such as Le Corbusier, Josep Lluís Sert or Eero Saarinen, and give back the extraordinary cultural network in which he moved.
Orani can tell something different, showing the genesis of that gaze, its anthropological reasons.

Here some of the central questions in his work stop being merely art-historical themes and acquire a concrete dimension. His relationship with matter refers back to the geology of his land, as well as to family experience and his father’s trade. The attention to community, the theme of participation, take on a crucial meaning. A museum in the place of origin has access to a memory that is not only documentary. There is an oral, vernacular, everyday memory, made of people who remember him or who have gathered the memory of previous generations. There are the light, the silences, the movement of the landscape: elements difficult to restore inside an exhibition, and they require a language, a narration, a rooted and conscious approach.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8phwlmm7eei6.jpg
content.caption: Model for the Monument to the Mason of Orani, from the Building Blocks series, 1955, concrete, 63.5 x 68.5 x 34.5 cm. Photo P. Pinna. Courtesy Museo Nivola

content.content: This does not mean reading Nivola exclusively through Sardinia: that would be equally reductive, because his artistic identity is born precisely from the encounter between Orani and the world. The strength of the Museo Nivola lies, if anything, in the possibility of holding these two dimensions together. On one side, an artist fully part of the international culture of the twentieth century; on the other, a biography and an imaginary profoundly rooted in the island.
Perhaps what the Museo Nivola can offer in a unique way is exactly the possibility of understanding that these two dimensions are not in contradiction.
The last question is about what comes next, and the answer describes something closer to a workshop than to a shrine.

Could you tell us, as far as possible, about your plans for the future and for the development of the Museo Nivola? We were particularly struck by the way the museum goes beyond the traditional exhibition space, creating a dialogue between art, architecture, landscape and the village of Orani. How do you imagine the next phase of its evolution?

The direction we are following is to deepen precisely this hybrid identity of the Museo Nivola: a monographic museum as a research centre, as a place dedicated to the contemporary, to architecture, to landscape, to education and, once again, to community.

The new programme Nivola vis-à-vis arises from that need. After a series of exhibitions dedicated to contemporary artists, our vision returns to questioning Nivola directly, placing him in relation with the figures, experiences and questions of his time. It is not a matter of simply constructing formal comparisons, but of analysing Nivola’s work as a point of departure for themes that are still vital and necessary: space and the body, architecture and design, the interpenetration of art and environment. The exhibition Nivola, Colombo e lo spazio intorno, currently on view, reflects for example on space as physical and relational cognition. Around it orbit important reflections on what Nivola’s research continues to suggest to the present. Which aspects of his work still appear open, urgent and productive? Within international debate, it is fundamental to reactivate their design potential, bringing back to the centre of current discourse the questions Nivola posed more than seventy years ago about the relationship between art and society, between education and imagination, between the project and everyday life.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8pvry22l32qj.jpg
content.caption: The permanent collection, Museo Nivola, Orani. Photo Cedric Dasesson. Courtesy Museo Nivola

content.content: In the coming months, this work will continue through a rereading of the permanent collection. The temporary departure of some works for the exhibition dedicated to Nivola at the Triennale di Milano will become an occasion to rethink the display, to return to studying the storerooms, to present lesser-known works and to create other connections. We want scientific research to be able to speak with educational activity, every exhibition to be able to generate an experience within public space, the heritage to be continuously reread through the “sentiment of the present”, and the museum to continue to be perceived by the community as a belonging.

It is a dynamic that, in the end, already belonged to Nivola: crossing the world without losing the bond with the place one set out from. And this is perhaps the model of museum we are interested in continuing to build: not a closed place that preserves a legacy, but an organism capable of putting it back into circulation, continuously.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt8phwxzw8tcdl.jpg
content.caption: Piazza Satta, Nuoro, 1967. Architect Richard Stein. Photo C. Nivola. Courtesy Museo Nivola

content.content: The exhibition Nivola, Colombo e lo spazio intorno is on view at the Museo Nivola in Orani, Sardinia. Works from the permanent collection will travel to the exhibition dedicated to Nivola at the Triennale di Milano, and the display in Orani will be rebuilt around their absence.

articles.title: Souv: The Souvenir That Doesn't Forget
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Matej Petrić and Antonio Šeparović on turning an ordinary fridge magnet into the entrance to a traveler's own photos, why nobody actually wants to buy NFC technology, and what it took to put a laser engraver in a startup that started as two friends and a third coffee in Zagreb.

content.content: Every souvenir shop sells the same promise: a small object that will remind you, years later, that you were somewhere. A magnet does this job better than almost anything else, which is exactly the problem. It remembers the fact of the trip and forgets everything that made the trip worth remembering – who you were laughing with on the ferry, what the light looked like on the last night, the wrong turn that became the best hour of the week. That richer material does not disappear. It is on your phone, buried a few thousand photographs deep, in the part of the camera roll nobody scrolls back to.

Souv, a startup out of Zagreb, was built to close exactly that gap. Tap a physical card or magnet with your phone – no app to install – and it opens a personal space tied to that specific place and trip: your own photographs, a short recap video, a note for later. The object stays on the fridge, doing what a souvenir has always done. The memory it points to stays reachable, which is the part that used to get lost.

The company started with two friends at university. Since a first pilot at a cycling event on the island of Brač, Souv has spread along the Croatian coast, into museum shops and chain retail, and has been named a finalist in the Digital Communication Design category of Zagreb Design Week 2026, where it will show at the Academy of Fine Arts this September.

We spoke with co-founders Matej Petrić and Antonio Šeparović about the third coffee in Zagreb that started it, the version of the idea they were sure would work and had to throw out anyway, and what it actually took to put colour-engraved stainless steel into production.

Take us back to the very beginning – was there a specific trip, a specific place, or a specific frustration that actually sparked the idea for Souv? Describe that moment in detail – where you were, what you were trying to do, and what wasn't working.
The funny thing is that Souv was not born on a beach, in an airport, or during some particularly dramatic trip. It started over coffee in Zagreb.

Antonio and I were sitting in WESPA, already on what he remembers as our third coffee, talking about how many photographs we take when we travel and how rarely we actually return to them afterwards. At the same time, our homes were full of physical reminders of places we had visited, especially magnets. The strange thing was that the physical object survived, while the actual experience was buried somewhere among thousands of photographs on a phone.
That disconnect became the starting point. We asked a very simple question: what if the physical souvenir could somehow carry the digital memories with it?

At first it sounded almost obvious. Tap a souvenir, open your photographs, add something about the place. Then we started asking the harder questions: what should the physical object actually be, why would someone buy it, how do you make the technology invisible, and how do you make something digital feel like a real keepsake rather than another app?

Who was on the founding team, and how did you split the early work between you? Looking back, whose idea ended up shaping the product the most, and did that person's role change once the company grew?

Souv was founded by the two of us, Matej Petrić and Antonio Šeparović. We were friends and university colleagues before becoming business partners, and both of us came from software and digital product backgrounds. That meant the early division of work was much less clean than “one technical founder and one business founder.” In the beginning, both of us were doing whatever the product needed.

I also would not honestly attribute Souv to one person's idea. The initial question came out of a conversation between us, and the product was shaped by iteration afterwards. If one principle influenced the product more than anything else, it was something we learned during testing: people are not interested in buying NFC technology.
They are interested in preserving an experience. Once we understood that, the technology became quieter and the memory became the centre of the product.

What did the very first version of Souv actually look like – the card, the app, the whole experience? Which parts of that first version survived into what's sold in stores today, and which parts got thrown out entirely, maybe even something you were sure would work?

The first versions were much closer to proofs of concept than to the Souv you can buy today. The basic idea was already there: a physical card or magnet with an NFC or QR connection that opened a digital space associated with that particular object. We needed to prove that the connection between an object on your desk or refrigerator and a personal digital memory could feel natural.

What survived is actually the most fundamental part of the idea. You still tap a physical object, nothing needs to be downloaded, and that object becomes the entrance to your own photographs, videos, notes and journey.

Almost everything around that core became more refined. The onboarding became simpler, the digital experience became much less technology-led, and the physical product developed into two very different expressions: an accessible printed Eco version and a Premium object made from brushed stainless steel with colour laser engraving.

One thing we initially overestimated was the “wow” of the technology itself. We assumed tapping an object with a phone would be the part people found most interesting. It is useful, but it is not the reason they care. The important moment is when they understand what is on the other side of the tap. That changed the way we designed and explained the entire product.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt919sg821bqcm.jpg
content.caption: Early sketches, a “Souvenirs with superpowers” flyer and a store display stand. Courtesy Souv

content.content: Walk us through the milestones that mattered most along the way – the first store, the first city outside your home base, Zagreb Design Week. For each one, what actually changed afterward – and was there a moment that felt bigger from the outside than it actually was on the inside, or the reverse?
There were several milestones, but they mattered for very different reasons.

The first time Souv was used in a real environment was particularly important. At the Uvati Vitar cycling event on Brač, participants received a personalised Souv as part of the event experience. Around 70% of the distributed Souvs were activated and filled with personal memories, and almost one in five participants shared the experience. The numbers were based on a small pilot, but internally that moment was much bigger than a press article or presentation because strangers were finally using the product without us standing next to them explaining it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt919s9royx1r6.jpg
content.caption: The first real-world use of Souv: a personalised card handed out at the Uvati Vitar cycling event on Brač. Courtesy Souv

content.content: The first retail location in Zagreb was another psychological shift. Until then Souv was something we had designed, tested and presented. Putting it into an actual shop meant a person who had never met us could see it on a shelf, understand it and decide whether it deserved their money.

There was not really one neat “second city” afterwards. The rollout moved quite quickly from Zagreb towards the coast, with Souv appearing across places including Split, Zadar, Dubrovnik, Šibenik, Pula, Poreč, Korčula and Brač. By August, the retail network included independent stores, museum locations and chain retail locations.

And now there is Zagreb Design Week. Souv has been selected as a finalist in the 2026 Digital Communication Design and Interaction Design category and will be exhibited at the Academy of Fine Arts from 15 to 20 September. That exhibition is still ahead of us, so we cannot pretend to know what it will change yet. But the selection itself means a lot because it recognises Souv not only as a tourism startup, but as a piece of interaction and communication design.

Interestingly, some of the moments that looked small from the outside, like watching people use Souv at the first event, felt enormous internally. Media exposure sometimes works the other way around: it looks like a major milestone publicly, while inside the company you are still thinking about the next production batch, a software bug or whether the display in a store is positioned correctly.

You call it 'not your typical souvenir.' Was there a particular souvenir – one you personally owned, bought, or were given – that you found genuinely disappointing, and did that specific object shape what Souv became?
There was not one terrible souvenir that made us say, “we have to fix this industry.”

It was almost the opposite. We actually like souvenirs, and particularly magnets, which is why the magnet became our first format. They work remarkably well as physical triggers. You see one on the refrigerator and immediately remember Dubrovnik, Paris or the island you visited five years ago.

The disappointment was that the object could only take you so far. It could tell you, “I was there,” but not what happened there, who you were travelling with, what made you laugh, or what the place actually felt like.
Meanwhile, all of that richer material existed. It was simply sitting somewhere on the 23,000-photo timeline of a phone.

So the object that influenced Souv was not one particularly bad souvenir. It was probably the very ordinary magnet that does its job quite well, placed next to a phone that contains the much better story but almost never tells it again. We wanted to connect those two things.

Each city – Zagreb, Dubrovnik, Split, Zadar, Brač, Korčula – has its own visual identity. Walk through how you actually decide what a new city's card should look and feel like, and has a local ever told you that you got their city wrong?
We try not to start with the question, “Which landmark should we put on this card?”

We start with what makes the place recognisable to the people who actually know it. That includes architecture and landmarks, of course, but also colour, local visual codes, landscape, small details, stories and the way the destination presents itself. Then we reduce that material into something that can work as an object rather than trying to fit an entire tourist brochure onto a magnet.

The design also has to survive the material. Something that looks beautiful on a screen may behave completely differently when UV printed on the Eco version or colour engraved into stainless steel, so the process moves continuously between visual design and physical testing.
Our art director Antonija has been central to developing that visual language, while destination partners give us local feedback before editions go into production.

And yes, locals have challenged details. Usually it is not a dramatic “you completely misunderstood our city” moment, but smaller corrections are extremely valuable. A motif can be technically recognisable and still feel wrong to someone who sees that place every day.
We would much rather have that conversation during development than produce a beautifully designed object that locals themselves do not believe represents them.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt919s1merprdg.jpg
content.caption: The visual language of a Souv card starts with what locals recognise, not with the nearest landmark. Courtesy Souv

content.content: Tap. Save. Relive your trip. Describe, step by step, what actually happens in the seconds right after someone taps a card for the first time – and then what typically happens weeks or months later, once they're back home. Do you know of a moment when it genuinely surprised or moved someone?
The first tap is deliberately simple.

You touch the Souv with an NFC-enabled phone, or scan the QR code on the back. The experience opens directly in the browser, so there is no app to install. On the first visit, you sign in, choose whether you are keeping the Souv for yourself or preparing it as a gift, and claim that particular Souv. From there you can add your first photographs, videos or message.

Once it has been claimed, it becomes your personal memory space. You can organise the journey through a timeline, continue adding material, create a recap video and explore selected content connected to the destination.

The more interesting part happens later. Weeks, months or even years after the trip, the physical object is still there. You see it on your desk or refrigerator and tap it again. Instead of opening a generic destination page, you return to your own photographs and your own version of that place.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt919sukn6i5qq.jpg
content.caption: Inside the tap: a trip timeline, shared memories and the map of where a Souv was made. Courtesy Souv

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt919sl1cg9g0o.jpg
content.caption: Early interface work for the claiming flow and the personal collection screen. Courtesy Souv

content.content: The next question is about the one part of the product that could not be solved by iterating on the app: a physical object, made in batches, that has to look the same the five-hundredth time as it did the first.

What's been the hardest part of building Souv so far? Pick one concrete example – a specific technical problem, a specific design decision, or a specific logistical headache – and walk through how you actually solved it, including anything you tried first that failed.
One very concrete example is the Premium stainless-steel Souv.
On paper, the idea sounded simple: take stainless steel and engrave the destination artwork in colour. In reality, producing that object consistently became one of the hardest parts of the project.

We tested different materials, engraving parameters, finishes, production speeds and ways of preparing the artwork. The difficulty was not producing one beautiful sample. You can spend an unreasonable amount of time making one piece look good. The real problem is creating the fiftieth or the five-hundredth piece with the same quality, within a production time and cost that makes sense for a retail product.

We repeatedly ran into trade-offs between visual quality, durability, repeatability and speed. Eventually we realised that we would not get the level of control we wanted if we treated production as a completely external black box.

So we brought a significant part of the process in-house and built our own small production setup in Zagreb. That was not part of the original startup plan. We came from software. Suddenly we were learning about stainless steel, lasers, material tolerances, finishing and production workflows.
In retrospect, that difficulty improved Souv. We now understand the physical object at a much deeper level because we were forced to learn how to make it ourselves.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt919sqhdw818b.jpg
content.caption: The Premium edition: colour laser engraving on brushed stainless steel. Courtesy Souv

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt919t7s2uwlyf.jpg
content.caption: An early version of the Souv product, from city artwork to the engraving bench. Courtesy Souv

content.content: The last question is about scale, and the answer turns out to be less about new cities than about what Souv actually is: an object, or a layer that any object could carry.

Where do you see Souv a few years from now? Is it mainly more cities and countries, a specific new feature you're already working on, or something about the product itself you'd genuinely want to change if you could start over?
A few years from now, we would like Souv to be much bigger than a collection of Croatian city magnets.

Croatia is the right place for us to prove the model because tourism is such an important part of everyday life here, but the underlying behaviour is universal. People travel, take hundreds of photographs, buy something to remember the trip and then rarely return to most of the digital material they created.
So international expansion is definitely part of the ambition, but the more important expansion is from a single product into a platform.

That means continuing to develop our own collectible Souv objects, but also allowing the Souv experience to live on other physical products. One direction we are already developing is a small NFC/QR Souv layer that can be integrated into an existing souvenir or its packaging. A ceramic object, book, museum product or locally made gift would not have to become “a Souv product”; it could keep its existing identity while gaining the personal memory experience behind it.
The digital side will keep growing as well: richer ways of organising journeys, gifting, collections, recap experiences and destination content that can evolve after the trip.
If we could start again, the biggest thing we would change is that we would begin with the emotional proposition much earlier and test real-world retail behaviour sooner.
In the beginning we spent too much time thinking like technologists. Today we know that the NFC, QR code and software should almost disappear.
The product is not really about tapping something with your phone. It is about giving an experience a physical place to live.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mt919t3r3yquvm.jpg
content.caption: Souvenirs that keep memories alive: travel, connect, relive. Courtesy Souv

articles.title: Nick Dahlen - A Contemporary Take on Modernism
articles.author: Maria Ivanova
articles.excerpt: An artist who transforms the beauty of everyday life into striking illustrations within his own visual world.

content.content: Nick Dahlen is an artist and illustrator from Minneapolis whose work revives the spirit of modernism through a contemporary lens.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtd1x28og4jut9.jpg

With a background in graffiti and a degree in Graphic Design, Dahlen has developed a visual language that combines the strength of modernist aesthetics with a sense of nostalgia – perhaps for a visual era we instinctively long for without even realizing it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtd22zg50cmc2s.jpg

The foundation of Dahlen’s style is remarkably consistent, and that consistency only makes it more compelling. Once you encounter one of his images, you immediately want to move on to the next, drawn in by the pleasure of clean, simplified forms covering otherwise ordinary, everyday subjects.
Style & Influences

This visual accessibility – in the best possible sense of the word – is largely created through saturated, contrasting shadows that immediately establish the contours of each form. We can read the scene effortlessly, and that clarity makes it instinctively appealing.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtd1xwmidgec86.jpg

The simplification of forms, combined with deliberate distortions and an authorial sense of proportion, recalls Cubism, particularly the work of Fernand Léger and Pablo Picasso. It is worth lingering on this idea of simplification because, in Dahlen’s work, it exists hand in hand with complexity. This dichotomy is rooted in the distortion of form and in a belief in its inherent plasticity.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtd1y7ryriiac0.jpg

The distortions – and particularly the enlarged proportions – make his figures feel monumental, almost sculptural. Here, one can trace an affinity with the work of Brazilian artist Tarsila do Amaral, whose figures similarly acquire a powerful, almost sculptural presence through their simplified and exaggerated forms.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtd1zyascjdrr3.jpg

Boldness is balanced by a certain fluidity, which keeps the work visually inviting. All of these elements come together through a palette of muted tones, transforming familiar subjects into instantly arresting compositions.

The visual impact happens almost immediately. Contrasting shadows and simplified figures allow us to read the image effortlessly, while simultaneously presenting a reimagined form of figurative painting.

Dahlen’s background in graphic design – particularly his attention to the visual language of twentieth-century posters – seems to have played an important role here. A strong awareness of hierarchy, direct communication, and the clear transmission of both image and meaning coexist with his distinctive treatment of form.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtd20y5thpnjgh.jpg
Subjects

Dahlen uses this visual language to depict ordinary objects and everyday scenes: preparing food, playing dominoes, cutting with scissors, assembling a puzzle. He has a particular fascination with food.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtd1xht1z7jkcw.jpg
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtd23vnikc0w6o.jpg

There is something striking about the way we can look at the same object every day, while an artist can present it to us in a way that feels completely unfamiliar – beyond the limits of our imagination.
Dahlen’s work ultimately seeks to communicate a sense of positive energy while subtly reflecting certain tensions and difficulties, leaving their interpretation to the symbolism of form and colour.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtd23kpm92lh8t.jpg

articles.title: Soft Modernism: Bryn and Ellefsen's Physics Building at Blindern
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: They won the competition with a Roman temple, went to look at what Europe was building, and came home to strip their own drawing bare. What stands at Blindern is functionalism that kept the brass, the colour and the curve.

content.content: The story modernism tells about itself is a story of conversion: the young architect sees the new work, throws out the mouldings and never looks back. Fysikkbygningen at Blindern is that story with the receipts attached, because both halves of it survive on paper. Finn Bryn and Johan Ellefsen won the University of Oslo competition in 1926 with a Roman temple: a columned facade in the centre, a round vestibule ringed by galleries, a dome on top, all of it in red brick and granite. Then they went to Germany, France and the Netherlands to see what was being built, came back and took their own drawing apart.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mted5ffo3rs7kw.jpg
content.caption: The physics building seen from the open field, Oslo, early 1950s. Photographer unknown, National Library of Norway, public domain

content.content: What they kept was the symmetry and the materials. What went was everything that made the building an argument about Rome. The tall windows dropped, the dome and the temple front disappeared, and the facade was regrouped into the harder geometry that stands there now. The building was finished in 1935 and opened in 1936, ten years after they won it, which means the design that made their reputation was quietly demolished by its own authors somewhere between the competition and the scaffolding.

It helps to remember what Blindern was at the time. Not a campus: a farm. The university had bought agricultural land north-west of the city and was moving out of its neoclassical quarter downtown, and the first buildings stood in a meadow with a dirt track running past them. There was no context to answer to, only a field, a brief and a decade that believed a building should be honest about its purpose.

alts: The approach to the physics building, late 1940s. National Library of Norway, public domain
The same front in 2009, with the garden grown in. Photograph: Kjetil Ree, CC BY-SA 3.0

content.content: Even stripped, the building reads as civic architecture rather than as a laboratory. A central tower rises out of a long horizontal block, its top floor cut open by a continuous band of glazing, and the brick is laid dark and warm rather than rendered white. Norwegian functionalism arrived through Sweden and Denmark rather than direct from Dessau, and it arrived softened: less manifesto, more craft, willing to keep the material a country already knew how to build with. Bryn and Ellefsen had been in partnership since 1922 and would go on to design the Norwegian pavilion for the 1939 World's Fair in New York.

alts: Nedre Blindern from the air, around 1955. Photograph: Fjellanger-Wideroe, Oslo Museum, CC BY-SA 4.0
The same ground in 2015, with the city grown around it. Photograph: GAD, CC BY-SA 4.0

content.content: The plan is disciplined where discipline pays. A physics faculty in the 1930s needed vibration-free floors, long service runs, blackout rooms and a lecture hall that could seat a generation of students, and the building solves all of it with the efficiency the period demanded. It housed chemistry too, until that institute moved out in the 1960s and the name shortened to the one it carries now. Then, at the point where circulation happens, where people actually meet the building, the geometry loosens. Stairs sweep rather than turn. Handrails are brass. Ceilings lift. Colour appears where a purist would have left plaster.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtectqskblakpa.jpg
content.caption: The glazed stair volume on the garden side, held in Virginia creeper. Photograph: Punkmorten, public domain

content.content: The vestibule is the whole argument in miniature, and it is the one room where the demolished 1926 scheme still shows through. Bryn and Ellefsen had promised a domed rotunda; what they built instead is a double-height hall with a black and white zigzag floor, closer to a 1930s ocean liner than to a laboratory, opening on both sides so that the space worked as a public passage between Majorstuen and the campus rather than as a lobby.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtectrdx02xngm.jpg
content.caption: The vestibule, looking towards the entrance. Photograph: Mysteriumen, CC BY-SA 3.0

content.content: Through the middle of it hangs a Foucault pendulum: a gilded ball bearing twenty centimetres across and weighing thirty-two kilograms, on a wire of 14.1 metres. Foucault's original in Paris in 1851 was a 28-kilogram weight on 67 metres of wire, the first demonstration in a room rather than a sky that the earth turns. At Oslo's latitude of sixty degrees north the plane of the swing takes 27 hours and 43 minutes to come back round. It is a working instrument and a piece of interior design at once, the one object here that explains the discipline housed in the building without a single word.

alts: The brass bob, the brass rail and the explanatory plate, over the star-cut stone floor. Photograph: Bernt Rostad, CC BY 2.0
The same bob in 2005, with the ring marking the swing. Photograph: Mads Bodker, CC BY 2.0

content.content: Above it, across three walls around the main entrance, Per Lasson Krohg painted 260 square metres of fresco with glass inlays and painted glass. He won that competition in 1935, the year the building was finished, and the work was completed in the autumn of 1938, paid for by the consul general Peter Krag. It is called Atomet i verdensrommet, the atom in space: the sun and the planets ringed by galaxies drawn as a woman and a man, with the aurora running through the composition. Krohg would later paint the mural in the United Nations Security Council chamber in New York.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtectrtx0buv71.jpg
content.caption: Atomet i verdensrommet, Per Krohg, completed 1938, on the eastern wall. Photograph: Bernt Rostad, CC BY 2.0

content.content: Note what that means for the chronology. The classical scheme was abandoned in the late twenties as too decorative for the new century, and then, with the functionalist building standing finished, the university ran a competition to cover its entrance in painted cosmology and hung a brass weight in the middle of it. The glazing bars of the stair window cut straight through the picture. The grid and the painting hold each other rather than compete, and the conservators from NIKU who cleaned the work in 2015 were maintaining something no purist reading of the 1930s can quite account for.

That is the reason the building still teaches something. The heroic version of the decade asks a structure to be honest, and honesty gets understood as bareness. Fysikkbygningen accepts every functional demand of its brief, drops its own columns to do so, and then treats warmth, colour and curvature as functional demands too, on the grounds that the people inside are also part of the programme. Nearly a century on, with the creeper turning scarlet over the entrance each October and the pendulum still swinging, it looks less like a compromise with modernism than a correction to it.

Sources

  • Museum for universitets- og vitenskapshistorie, UiO – the 1926 winning entry, the study trip and how the temple facade was removed – muv.uio.no
  • Museum for universitets- og vitenskapshistorie, UiO – Bryn and Ellefsen at Nedre Blindern: the practice and the campus plan – muv.uio.no
  • Store norske leksikon – Finn Bryn: the partnership from 1922 and the later work – snl.no
  • Fysisk institutt, UiO – the pendulum in the vestibule: 32 kg gilded bob, 14.1 m wire, 27 h 43 min at 60 degrees north – mn.uio.no
  • Paragone – Atomet i verdensrommet: the 1935 art competition, 260 square metres, completed autumn 1938, conserved by NIKU in 2015 – paragone.no
  • Nasjonalmuseet – Bryn and Ellefsen, original competition drawings for the physics building – nasjonalmuseet.no
Photographs: freely licensed via Wikimedia Commons, each credited in its caption. Archive views from the National Library of Norway and Oslo Museum.

articles.title: Where the Warmth Lives: How Two Traditions Measured the Turn from Summer to Autumn
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Autumn does not make the light warmer. Measured region by region, two canvases of the same field show the sky staying where it was while the ground swings seventeen points warm, and the shadows, all summer filled with blue skylight, turn into the warmest passages in the picture. With three pastels in which the medium is held still and only the season moves. And a second half in which autumn is not a light at all: a calendar that declares it on the seventh of August, a season carried by one grass, and a moon with no horizon to rise from.

content.content: The usual way to describe autumn in painting is to say that the light turns warm. It is the wrong description, and a series of measurements taken from the paintings themselves shows why. The light does not turn warm. The ground does, and once it does, it takes over the job the sky had been doing all summer. What changes is not the colour of the light but the address of the warmth in the picture.

This piece works through that claim on ten paintings and pastels, most of them measured region by region: two canvases of the same field before and after the turn, three pastels in which the medium is held constant and only the season moves, and a set of comparisons that ends somewhere useful for anyone who paints, photographs or simply looks.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgsb1705nao6y.jpg
content.caption: Claude Monet. Stacks of Wheat (End of Summer), 1890 to 1891. Oil on canvas, 60 by 100.5 cm. Art Institute of Chicago, gift of Arthur M. Wood, Sr. in memory of Pauline Palmer Wood.

content.content: One field, twice

In 1890 and 1891 Monet painted the wheat stacks in a field a few minutes from his house at Giverny, returning to the same shapes at different hours and in different weather. Six of those canvases are in the Art Institute of Chicago. That makes it possible to compare not two subjects but one subject twice, with everything except the season held still: same field, same stacks, same painter, same distance, same box of colours.

We measured four regions in each canvas: a strip of sky across the top, the band of trees at the horizon, the foreground field, and the body of the large stack. The measure is simple, the red channel minus the blue channel, which is a serviceable proxy for whether a passage leans warm or cool. Positive means warm.

Sky: minus 3.9 in late summer, plus 1.6 in autumn. Almost no movement.
Treeline: plus 22.4, then plus 10.7. The distance gets cooler, not warmer.
Foreground field: plus 1.0, then plus 18.2. A swing of seventeen points.
The large stack: plus 36.9, then plus 47.6.

The sky is not the variable. The field is. Between the two canvases the ground moves from neutral to distinctly warm while the sky stays where it was, and the horizon actually goes bluer as thicker air pushes the far trees back. Whatever the season is doing, it is doing it at ground level.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgsb1s5cdzb0h.jpg
content.caption: Claude Monet. Stacks of Wheat (End of Day, Autumn), 1890 to 1891. Oil on canvas, 65.8 by 101 cm. Art Institute of Chicago, Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection.

content.content: The same square metre, close up
Crop the identical patch out of both canvases, the foot of the large stack and the field running away from it, and enlarge it. This is where the argument stops being a table of numbers.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgssxdiwdvy1y.jpg
content.caption: End of Summer, detail. The stubble is built from blue, violet and turquoise strokes with pink and yellow-green flecks laid between them.

content.content: In the summer detail the field is blue. Not blue-ish: in the lower strip of this crop, 26.5 per cent of the surface sits in the blue and violet band and only 13.5 per cent in the rose and red. The stubble is drawn in short chopped strokes running in three or four directions, each one a separate decision, with the canvas breathing between them. The stack sits on that cool ground as a warm object, and the contrast between them is the subject.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgssxxm2w54lw.jpg
content.caption: End of Day, Autumn, detail of the same passage. Blue has fallen to 0.6 per cent of the strip; rose and red have risen to 37.2.

content.content: In the autumn detail the blue is gone. Six tenths of one per cent of that same strip is still blue or violet, against 37.2 per cent rose and red. The handling has changed with it: the strokes are longer, dragged more horizontally, and the paint has become a continuous crust rather than a mesh of separate marks. The stack and the field are now the same temperature, plus 47.6 against plus 18.6, and the picture has lost the contrast that organised the summer version. It has to be organised by something else, and Monet organises it by value, the dark mass of the stack against a pale field, and by the one surviving cold note along the treeline.
Why the warmth moves

The mechanism is not mysterious once the numbers point at the ground. Any shadow is lit by whatever the sky and the surroundings bounce into it. In high summer, with a high sun and a large area of clear sky, the dominant fill light is skylight, which is blue, and shadows go blue. That is the physical basis of the whole Impressionist habit of painting violet shadows on a green field. It is not a stylistic tic; it is a measurement.

By late October two things have changed. The sky is more often a diffuser than a source, an even grey ceiling with no strong directional beam and no strong blue. And the ground under everything has turned into an enormous warm reflector: dry stubble, fallen leaves, bare soil, all of it ochre. The secondary light in the landscape stops being blue and becomes orange. The shadow, which is nothing but secondary light, warms up accordingly.

Measured across the whole set, this reversal is the most consistent thing we found. In Boudin's summer sky study the darkest fifth of the picture is 24.8 points cooler than neutral and the lightest fifth is 11.4 points warmer: a gap of 36 points in the textbook direction. In Lhermitte's October river the relationship is inverted, the shadows warmer than the lights by 45 points. Levitan's Golden Autumn: inverted by 20. Monet's own two canvases move from a gap of 0.4 to a gap of 7.6 in the same direction.
Summer keeps its warmth in the light and its coolness in the shadow. Autumn does the opposite. The season is not a change of colour, it is a change of where the colour lives.
Against the word muted

Autumn is habitually called muted, and the paintings disagree. Mean saturation in Monet's late summer canvas is 0.169; in the autumn canvas it is 0.204. At the ninetieth percentile, that is, in the most intense tenth of the surface, the figures are 0.312 and 0.372. The autumn picture is the more saturated of the two by roughly a fifth.

What actually narrows is the hue range, not the intensity. The palette closes toward a smaller arc of the colour wheel and then works harder inside it. Jean-Charles Cazin's October Day is the limit case: measured across its whole surface it contains no green at all, 54 per cent yellow and ochre, 46 per cent orange and red, and a warm bias of 61 points, five times Monet's late summer. It is not a quiet picture. It is a loud picture made of three colours.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgsb3eugamqxr.jpg
content.caption: Jean-Charles Cazin. October Day, 1890 to 1893. Oil on canvas, 38.4 by 46.7 cm. Art Institute of Chicago, Henry Field Memorial Collection. No green anywhere on the surface.

content.content: Which colours survive the closing is worth noticing. Ochre, raw and burnt sienna, umber, red earth. These are the oldest pigments in use anywhere, ground out of the ground, in the caves tens of thousands of years before anyone had a blue that did not cost more than the panel it went on. Autumn returns painting to its first palette, and paints the season in the colours of the material it is depicting.
Where the yellow comes from, and why the red behaves differently

A green leaf is not green because green has been added. It is green because chlorophyll is dominant, and the carotenoids and xanthophylls that give the yellows and yellow-oranges have been sitting inside the leaf all summer, masked. When the tree begins withdrawing nutrients and chlorophyll production stops, the mask lifts and the yellow is revealed. It arrives by subtraction.

The reds are a different event. In many species anthocyanins are manufactured in autumn, made new in the leaf as sugars are trapped there by the closing of the vascular channels. So the two halves of the autumn palette come from opposite processes, one an unmasking and one a production, and this shows up in how they distribute. The yellows spread evenly through a whole mass of foliage, because they were already everywhere. The reds appear in patches: on particular trees, on the sunlit side, in the crown before the base. A painter who spreads red evenly through a wood has painted something that does not happen.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgsb6am3359k5.jpg
content.caption: Jean-Francois Millet. Haystacks: Autumn, about 1874. Oil on canvas. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Open Access. Measured here: the sky reads 105, 109, 97 and the ground 131, 104, 61. The field is brighter than the sky above it.

content.content: Millet's picture contains the other autumn inversion, the one that follows from the first. Under a diffusing overcast, a field of cut stubble becomes the brightest surface in view and the sky above it goes dull. In a summer landscape this is close to impossible, because the sky is the source. Here the source has been spread out and the ground is doing the reflecting, so the picture is effectively lit from below. It also solves an old compositional problem: the figure no longer has to compete with a brilliant sky and can be drawn as a dark shape on a bright ground.
Pastel, and why this season belongs to it

If one medium owns the three weeks of the turn, it is pastel, and the reason is optical rather than sentimental. Oil paint is pigment suspended in a film: light enters the film, is partly absorbed inside it, and comes back out having been changed on the way. That is what gives oil its depth and its capacity to be glazed. Pastel is pigment with almost no binder, a little gum, pressed into a stick and then abraded onto a toothed surface. It sits there as loose grains with air between them. Light does not travel through a medium; it scatters off the surfaces of dry particles and returns immediately, in all directions, with almost no specular component.

That is, in the exact optical sense, the same behaviour as an overcast autumn sky, which is a diffuser rather than a source. Pastel does not imitate the light of the season. It reproduces its physics.
Three pastels make the case better than any argument, because the medium is held constant and only the season moves. All three are drawn on toned paper, which is the second half of the story.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgssyf5sub0kk.jpg
content.caption: Eugene Boudin. Seascape with Open Sky, 1860. Pastel on grey wove paper mounted on board. Cleveland Museum of Art, CC0. Measured: the darkest fifth of this sheet is 24.8 points cooler than neutral, the widest cool-shadow gap in our entire set.

content.content: Boudin is the summer state of affairs in its purest form. He made hundreds of these sky studies on the Normandy coast, dated and timed on the sheet like meteorological records, and Corot called him the king of skies for it. What the measurement finds is exactly the summer signature: brilliant lights, and shadows filled with blue from an enormous open sky. The grey of the paper is doing the work of the middle tone, and the white chalk is spent only on the cloud tops.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgssyz6rhlac1.jpg
content.caption: John Henry Twachtman. Pastures, Branchville, Connecticut, about 1888 to 1891. Pastel on composition board. Cleveland Museum of Art, CC0.

content.content: Twachtman shows the second thing pastel can do that oil cannot. Almost nothing here is drawn. The tan of the support is the dry grass, the light and the season all at once, and the pastel is spent only on what departs from it: the dark trees at the left, the blue-violet shadows raking across the middle distance, a few strokes of white cloud, some surviving green. The artist chose the colour of the light before making a single mark, and then made as few marks as possible. In oil that ground would have vanished under the picture.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgsszdax0jzq1.jpg
content.caption: Leon Augustin Lhermitte. Quai au Sable, Chartèves, 1904. Pastel on grey wove paper. Cleveland Museum of Art, CC0. Shadows 52 points warm, lights 6.6: the reversal at its most extreme in our set.

content.content: And Lhermitte is the autumn state, in the same medium, on the same kind of toned sheet. Yellow poplars, a bank of ochre mud, a cold river holding the last blue in the picture, and shadows that are the warmest passages on the sheet by a distance of 45 points. Put the Boudin and the Lhermitte side by side and the entire argument of this piece is visible in two objects made of the same dust.

There is one more consequence of the medium worth stating, because it explains why pastel suits a transition specifically. A pastel cannot be repaired the way an oil can. There is no glaze, no scumble over a dried layer, no lifting with turpentine, no painting out. A passage from one colour to the next has to be built by laying dust over dust and by stumping, that is, by rubbing the pigment into the tooth of the paper with a rolled paper stub until one hue hands over to the next.
